explain.say: A hoverfly has no sting at all, but it wears the same black and yellow pattern. Birds that have learnt to fear wasps leave it alone too. This is called Batesian mimicry.

explain.say: The trick works best when mimics are rarer than the dangerous models. If there were more hoverflies than wasps, birds would learn that stripes are often safe to eat.

explain.say: You can spot the copy: wasps have four wings and long antennae, hoverflies have two wings and short antennae, and they hover in one spot. Other mimics include harmless snakes that copy coral snakes.

faq.a: Batesian mimicry is when a harmless animal copies the warning signals of a harmful one, so predators avoid it. It is named after Henry Walter Bates, who studied Amazon butterflies in the 1800s.

faq.q: How can you tell a hoverfly from a wasp?
faq.a: Hoverflies have one pair of wings, short stubby antennae and big eyes, and they hover still in the air. Wasps have two pairs of wings, long antennae and a narrow waist.

faq.q: Why must mimics be rarer than the animals they copy?
faq.a: If predators mostly met harmless mimics, they would learn the warning was a bluff and start eating striped insects. When the dangerous models are common, the lesson sticks.
asks: Can there be too many mimics?

faq.a: Mullerian mimicry is when two or more harmful species look alike, such as different stinging wasps and bees all with black and yellow bands. Predators learn one warning that protects them all.
asks: Do dangerous animals copy each other?

faq.a: Harmless milk snakes and scarlet kingsnakes copy venomous coral snakes, some caterpillars puff up to look like snakes, and some spiders look and walk like ants to avoid predators.
asks: Can a caterpillar look like a snake?

facts: Batesian mimicry is named after the naturalist Henry Walter Bates, who described it in 1862 from butterflies in the Amazon.
Hoverflies are true flies with two wings, while wasps have four.

quiz.say: Why do birds avoid hoverflies, even though they cannot sting?

options.show: Hoverflies are too fast to catch
options.say: Hoverflies are too fast to catch

quiz.why: Birds that learnt to fear wasps avoid the look-alike hoverfly too: Batesian mimicry.

wrong.1: Taste is not the protection; the warning look is.
wrong.2: Speed helps a little, but the copied colours are the key.
